h1: Corner welding machines — 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-axis TIG and plasma corner welders for bent boxes
intro: A corner welding machine welds the corners of bent sheet-metal parts — boxes, cabinets, trays, enclosures, doors — with the torch driven by the machine at a set speed instead of by hand, so every corner comes out the same and the welder is free while it runs. NovoTech sells the corner welders of GECAM, built in Parma, Italy, from one axis to four: the part is clamped from inside against copper guides that hold the corner square and draw off the heat, the TIG or plasma torch welds at 0 to 47 in/min, and the parameters of every part are stored. One axis welds a straight corner seam — the CWS 200 and CWS 300 on parts to 59″ square, the WELCOR 400 X on corners to 15-3/4″ high; two and three axes weld a seam that runs in two or three directions in one cycle; the four-axis WELCOR adds torch rotation and a laser that reads the seam before welding. Mild steel, stainless steel and aluminum. The welded corner then goes to a corner grinder. Supplied with a CSA-approved panel, installed and supported from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.q: What does a corner welding machine do?
faq.a: It welds the corner seam of a bent part with the torch driven by the machine at a set speed: the operator places the part with its corner against the copper squaring guide, locks it with a button and presses start. The result is a straight, even weld on every corner whatever the operator's skill, and the welder can prepare the next part while it runs.

faq.q: 1, 2, 3 or 4 axes — which do I need?
faq.a: One axis welds a straight corner seam — the corner of a plain box, up to 7-7/8″ high on the CWS 200, 11-13/16″ on the CWS 300 and 15-3/4″ on the WELCOR 400 X. On two axes (X and Y) the torch is driven in two directions: the WELCOR 400 XY welds seams up to 15-3/4″ on X and 4-5/16″ on Y. Three axes add Z — up to 1-15/16″ — so a seam that runs in three directions is welded in one cycle. The four-axis WELCOR adds torch rotation, from vertical to about 120°, and a laser that checks the edges and memorizes the path before welding. Send us a drawing of your part and we will tell you which one it needs.

faq.q: What do the copper groups do?
faq.a: The part is pressed from inside against copper — an outer unit 7-7/8″ or 11-13/16″ high and an inner unit from 1-15/16″ to 11-13/16″ chosen for the corner on the CWS and the WELCOR 400 to three axes; modular aluminum and copper pads from 3/8″ to 7-7/8″ thick, matched to the box, on the four-axis WELCOR. They hold the corner square during welding and draw the heat away, keeping the heat of the part down; cooled inner groups are recommended to avoid dark marks on the parts.

faq.q: How must the corner be bent?
faq.a: The two edges should meet on the corner — .0004″ (0.01 mm) apart and centred on it. Where the bend does not allow it, they may overlap by half the sheet thickness at most; on the CWS the gap between the edges must not exceed .008″ (0.2 mm). Good press brake work upstream pays off at the welder.

faq.q: TIG or plasma — and is the power source included?
faq.a: The machines work with a TIG or a plasma welding power source, which is not included. GECAM offers the Lorch T 250 — T 250 DC for mild and stainless steel, T 250 AC/DC also for aluminum — with a cooling unit and a torch group with a 9′10″ cable. Tell us the material, thickness and corner you weld and we will quote the machine with its power source.

Bent parts from 3-15/16 × 3-15/16″ to 59-1/16 × 59-1/16″ on the CWS 200, CWS 300 and CWS 300 XY (32-5/16″ square work table, 39-3/8″ to order), and to 39-3/8 × 39-3/8″ on the WELCOR 400 — on the four-axis the smallest box 1-15/16″ high. Mild steel, stainless steel and aluminum.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models whose main motor is 2.2 kW (3 HP) or less — a machine with a motor above 2.2 kW must run on three-phase power and cannot be converted to 240 V single-phase. Manual machines have no electrics.

origin_feature.title: Made in Italy by Gecam
origin_feature.text: Gecam designs and builds deburring, grinding and finishing machines at Vicofertile, Parma — 100 % made in Italy, with components from Italian suppliers within 125 miles (200 km) of the plant. In 2005 it took over Eurofintec, the abrasive-belt machine builder whose name its pipe and belt machines still carry.
